Deputy Governor's Keynote Address at the Oil and Gas Funding Forum 2013
Speaker
: Muhammad bin Ibrahim, FCB
Venue
: Sasana Kijang, Kuala Lumpur
Delivery Date
:
11 Jun. 2013
Terlebih dahulu, saya ingin merakamkan penghargaan kepada Malaysian Petroleum Resource Corporation kerana telah menjemput saya untuk menyampaikan sepatah dua kata pada persidangan “Oil and Gas Funding Forum 2013" ini. Saya juga ingin mengalu-alukan kedatangan tuan-tuan dan puan-puan pada hari ini. Penganjuran forum ini di Sasana Kijang adalah bertepatan dengan aspirasi dan komitmen Bank Negara Malaysia untuk menjadikan Sasana Kijang sebagai sebuah pusat pertemuan minda dan kolaborasi utama di kalangan pemain-pemain industri kewangan.
Building on the progress achieved over the last decade, the Malaysian financial sector is well positioned to continue to play an important role in financial intermediation through effective channelling of funds into productive sectors. As Malaysia advances into the next phase of economic development towards becoming a high-income, high value-added economy, the ability of the financial sector to continuously innovate and provide comprehensive and effective financial solutions to support strategic sectors like the oil and gas industry in Malaysia is no longer an option, but more of a necessity.
It is therefore my great pleasure to be here today to speak at the Oil and Gas Funding Forum 2013 organised by the Malaysian Petroleum Resource Corporation. This forum brings together key industry players from the oil and gas sector and provides an important opportunity for the leaders in this sector to interact and exchange ideas with the financial institutions on sustainable financing opportunities for the oil and gas industry. My remarks today will hence focus on the prospects for further growth for the oil and gas industry and the vibrant financing ecosystem that is currently available in Malaysia. I will also share some thoughts on the imperatives for the financial sector in order to be able to continuously support this sector moving forward.
Strong growth potential of the oil and gas industry
The global oil and gas production has grown by around 1.5% annually in the last decade, driven by rising demand from the rapidly developing countries, notably China, India and Southeast Asia. Oil demand from these emerging economies has in fact overtaken demand from industrialised countries given the growing affluence of the population in emerging economies. These developments which have tipped the global consumption of oil and gas geographically is expected to continue. Based on a report by the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), oil demand globally is expected to increase to 107 million barrels per day (mb/d) by 2035, from 87 mb/d in 2010. Of this amount, 87% of the growth in oil demand will come from emerging economies in Asia.
Malaysia, given its close proximity and increasing economic interlinkages with global energy consumers in Asia such as China and India, is well positioned to reap benefits from the increased demand for oil and gas. In 2012, the export of oil and gas from Malaysia increased to 19.8% of total exports, from 9.3% in 2000. The significant growth reflects the immense contribution of the oil and gas industry to the Malaysian economy, where the oil and gas sector accounted for 20% of GDP in 2012. In terms of contribution to the Government revenue, the oil and gas sector accounts for 35% of the total Government revenue for the period of 2011-2012 through dividend and corporate income tax payments as well as sales tax and export duty collected. The contribution of the oil and gas sector to the economy is also evident from the spill-over benefits to the other services sectors, namely transportation, construction and financial services. Additionally, it is encouraging to note that the Malaysian oil and gas companies have been venturing abroad, with the net investments abroad by oil and gas companies totalling RM 20 billion as at end 2012.
Given the importance of the oil and gas sector to the Malaysian economy, the Government has in the past provided various incentives and infrastructure to support this industry. Under the National Key Economic Areas (NKEA), the Government has identified the oil, gas and energy sector as one the main drivers of the economy and has implemented several initiatives under the Economic Transformation Programme (ETP) to further boost the development of this industry. The ETP estimates that oil and gas sector will raise the total gross national income contribution to RM241 billion by 2020 with greater participation by the private sector. This is more than a 100% increase in gross national income received from the oil and gas industry prior to 2009.
Recently, as part of the broader effort to diversify the economy and accelerate new sources of growth, the Government has reduced the tax rate for companies involved in the development of marginal oil fields from 38% to 25%, and has also launched the Global Incentives for Trading (GIFT) programme to encourage global companies trading in petroleum and petroleum related products to locate their regional operations to Malaysia. Under the programme, LNG trading companies that sign up before end-2014 is granted 100% income tax exemption on statutory income for the first 3 years of operations while companies involved in other petroleum-related commodities will enjoy a flat rate of 3% income tax. These fiscal incentives are expected to further spur the development of the oil and gas industry in Malaysia.
Vibrant financing ecosystem
For the oil and gas industry to meet its intended role as a strong contributor to economic growth, it is crucial that the financial sector is able to continuously innovate to better intermediate funds to this industry effectively and efficiently. Although the current financing ecosystem remains supportive to meet the needs of this sector, there is still capacity within the financial system to boost financing to the oil and gas industry. Allow me to share some statistics on current financing granted to this industry, and three observations on how the Malaysian financial system can play a larger role in supporting the growth and development of this industry, particularly to achieve the deliverables envisaged under the ETP.
As at end-2012, the total loans financed by the banking sector to the oil and gas industry amounted to RM5.4 billion, an increase of 65.5% from 2011. In fact, financing to this industry has been growing at an average annual rate of 67.7% since 2006. This include financing of activities incidental to extraction of crude oil and natural gas. The domestic bond market has also been mobilising funds for this sector, with outstanding ringgit-denominated bonds amounting to RM 2.1 billion as at end-2012. In terms of foreign currency-denominated bonds issued by the oil and gas sector, it is much larger. For example, the foreign currency-denominated bonds issued by four large oil and gas companies amounted to USD 9 billion as at end-2012.
In 2012, the services sector contributed 3.5 % of GDP growth and has emerged as one of the key contributors to growth over the last few years. The prospect for growth for support services activities in the oil and gas sector value chain is expected to expand with the increase in private investment activity and capital spending. The potential for growth in the oilfield and engineering support services for instance, is immense as the need for more technologically-advanced capabilities is required in areas such as enhanced oil recovery and deepwater exploration.
Towards this end, it is critical for the financial industry to channel adequate financing for these companies to support their continued growth and expansion. I certainly see room for the financial industry to enhance their capabilities to better anticipate and assess the financing needs of companies providing services in the oil and gas sector. For some of these activities, traditional bank lending may not be the best or even the appropriate solution.
Moving forward, there are sizeable opportunities for the financial sector to support the needs of this industry. Firstly, Islamic financial products offer a valuable proposition for enterprises seeking end-to-end Shariah compliant business financing. While Islamic financing today is largely carried out through non-participatory contracts such as mark-up sale (murabahah) and lease-based (ijarah) structures, the wider use of risk-sharing and participatory Islamic finance contracts such as the mudharabah and musyarakah structures in the future will provide a natural financing option to support the growth and development of the oil and gas industry, particularly for the smaller downstream companies. These profit-sharing and loss-bearing contractual agreements between the financier and entrepreneur would provide stronger incentives for both parties to ensure the success of the investment. Experience has shown that Islamic financing has demonstrated that its agile, competitive and cost-effective in funding wide spectrum of complex projects, and I believe that Islamic finance has the capacity to finance the oil and gas sector.
Besides financing alternatives mentioned earlier, there are also ample opportunities for the oil and gas industry to raise funds via the sukuk market. In fact, the first issuance of sukuk in the world was by Shell MDS to finance its oil and gas activities in Malaysia in 1990. Since then, many oil and gas companies have explored using sukuk as a mode of financing. One of the key milestones was the first “Emas" sukuk amounting to USD1.5 billion that was issued by Petronas in 2009. “Emas" is Malaysia's designation accorded to foreign currency denominated bonds and sukuk originating from Malaysia in the global capital market. Today, Malaysia continues to strengthen its position as an international Islamic finance marketplace and remains a key market place for sukuk issuances globally. As at end-2012, the total sukuk issued in Malaysia accounted for 74% of total global sukuk outstanding, with Malaysia having one of the largest US dollar denominated sukuk market worldwide.
Secondly, private equity financing can also play an important role in meeting the funding needs of start-ups, small downstream and midstream companies with growth potential in the oil and gas industry. Many of these smaller companies, which are important components in the national oil and gas value chain, may face difficulties sourcing for funds from the banking sector due to their less established track record and experience in the industry. Given that the industry is capital intensive, require highly specialized skill sets and experience and with proportionately higher risk of loss, the financiers to this industry would naturally expect to be more guarded to safeguard their interests. This is where private equity financiers can step in to bridge the gap in funding for these companies. Typically, these private equity financiers would originate from the sector, with specialized skills, know-how and experience to understand the commercial and sustainability aspects of the projects and the risks and challenges of the industry.
Thirdly, Malaysia's financial system that has become more regional and international can serve as an important conduit to facilitate business expansion abroad. Domestic businesses that venture abroad now have better access to financing and financial services provided by Malaysian banks with presence abroad. To date, six out of the eight banking groups have presence in 21 countries with substantial overseas operations centred in Southeast Asia. A few of these banking groups have successfully emerged as leading regional players, with an important role in contributing to the overall economic development of the region. With the larger network abroad, Malaysian banks are well positioned to facilitate intra-regional trade and investments, including in the oil and gas sector where the growth prospects of this sector are strong.
I pose a challenge for all who are present today, from the oil and gas players, financial services providers as well as consultants to work together to collectively come up with new and innovative funding solutions, taking on board the financial infrastructure that has been built over the years, such as the bond and sukuk markets, project financing and Islamic financing frameworks to finance the further expansion of the industry.
Imperatives for the financial institutions moving forward
While it is recognised that financial institutions have an important enabler and catalytic role to support economic growth, lessons from the recent global financial crisis have reinforced the importance of managing risk effectively to ensure financial stability and the effective functioning of financial intermediation is continuously preserved. The disproportionate growth of the financial sectors beyond the growth of the real economies has led to severe and profound ramifications to the real economies that would take many years to unwind and recover. At the international level, regulatory reforms are being widely debated, it is expected the outcome would significantly strengthen the regulation and supervision of financial institutions. A clear policy challenge ahead for regulators globally is to construct policy objectives and strategies that not only enhance stability for the future, but also to continuously support economic growth and creation of jobs. In this respect, a few imperatives must be present; supply of credits should not be disrupted especially to trade financing, infrastructure projects, SMEs and small businesses, regulatory and compliance costs should not caused increased in price of credits and regulatory framework should reflect the risks of our banking system, and not of the developed markets.
To my mind, there are two fundamental issues for financial institutions to consider when assessing financial relationships with businesses, in particular enterprises in the oil and gas industry.
Firstly, something simple should not be turned into something complex or difficult to comprehend. Banking products should be easily understood. There should be increased transparency in financial institutions' business activities, with the growth of financial activities firmly anchored to real economic activities. The recent global financial crisis provides a distinct example of how excessive leverage and exponential growth in financial activities that are detached from the growth of the real economy can become a source of widespread instability. An example, in 2011, combined data from the US NYMEX and ICE EUROPE indicated that the total volume for oil futures traded was 288 billion barrels per year valued at USD28 trillion, in contrast, global oil consumption was only 32 billion barrels per year or USD 32 billion. That means oil futures volume was more than 9 times the total volume of consumption. The reckless use of financial derivatives with oil treated as an asset class in recent years have led to greater speculative activities in the financial markets which in turn have contributed to the increased volatility of oil prices. The excessive speculation has decoupled price movements from the real fundamentals, affecting the growth of the real economy and diverting scarce capital from more productive economic ventures.
It is hence clear that such risky and highly leveraged undertakings are not productive and sustainable in the long run. At the core of its intermediary role, the primary purpose of financial institutions is to serve as an enabler and facilitate effective intermediation by matching savings and investments for the purpose of supporting real economic activities and contributing to economic growth. Financial institutions should therefore and ought to continue to focus on serving the real needs of the economy in an effective, efficient and responsible manner. It is my view that ensuring a close link between financial transactions and the real economy is fundamental in promoting economic and financial stability and it is in the interest of the financial institutions' long-term sustainability.
Secondly, financial institutions need to continuously enhance their capacity and capability to assess and manage risk. This is particularly important as financial institutions become more exposed to lending to smaller downstream and mid-stream companies in the oil and gas value chain. Traditional methods of credit assessment may need to be reviewed to take into account the innovation and capital intensive aspects of these businesses. The failure of several large and traditionally sound financial institutions during the global financial crisis has provided important lessons on the perils of lack of understanding on the inherent risks of financial products and poor transparency in financial dealings and emphasizing short-term gains against long-term sustainability. Strong risks management standards and practices supported by sound governance structures are hence important pre-requisites for financial institutions to build a profitable yet sustainable business especially as they embark on new areas of growth to support economic activities.
Central to this is the enhanced expectations on the Boards of financial institutions, where they have a critical role to play to ensure effective alignment and implementation of risk management policies and capital management strategies that commensurate with the business strategy of the financial institutions. This is even more critical in an environment where prescriptive-based regulations are gradually replaced with principle-based regulations to cater to the increasingly complex financial system.
Over the last 35 years, the oil and gas industry has grown by leaps and bounds. This is especially true in the case of Petronas that was formed in 1974 and grown into a company with an assets size of more than RM500 billion with operations in more than 30 countries. The corporation now is also one of the most profitable company in the world. A well-known international business newspaper described Petronas as 'a new seven sisters' reflecting the groups' influence in the oil and gas industry outside the OECD. Petronas's 5-year capital expenditure programmes of RM300 billion [of which 60% would be invested domestically] would significantly transform the oil and gas landscape in the country. The RAPID project value alone is estimated at RM60 billion. There are other downstream projects such as the Fertiliser Plant in Sabah, the Regasssification terminal in Melaka, Lahad Datu and Southern Johore and the Floating LNG Project. With these projects, lies the opportunities, not only for the banks but also for the capital market players. The challenge is whether Malaysian financial services industry have the capacity, the skills and the experience to tap into the opportunities of the ever expanding oil and gas industry.
Conclusion
There are tremendous opportunities for the oil and gas industry to collaborate with the financial industry to create a vibrant and sustainable financing ecosystem that is conducive for its growth and development. The financial industry at this juncture is undergoing a new trajectory of transformation and growth that will enable it to support Malaysia's transition towards a high value added, high income economy. For the oil and gas players, I also understand that there are heavy priorities ahead in the area of efficient management of funds and resources and strengthened research and development capabilities. These are critical agendas to further sharpen the competitive edge of the industry and to enable it to thrive and flourish at the next stage of development. It is hence timely for continuous dialogue between the oil and gas industry and the financial industry to ensure that the financial needs of the oil and gas industry are adequately met. Deeper understanding of the operations, risks and challenges faced by the oil and gas industry can certainly pave the way for better support from the financial industry.
On that note, I wish you an engaging and productive conference.
title: Deputy Governor's Keynote Address at the Oil and Gas Funding Forum 2013

Governor’s Welcoming Address at the 10th IFSB Summit 2013 - The Future of the Islamic Financial Services Industry: Resilience, Stability and Inclusive Growth
Speaker
: Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz
Venue
: Sasana Kijang
Delivery Date
:
16 May. 2013
“Raising the Bar for the Next Phase of Growth and Development - Sustaining Transformative Momentum”
It is a great pleasure to welcome you to this 10th IFSB Summit, on the ‘
The Future of the Islamic Financial Services Industry: Resilience, Stability and Inclusive Growth’.
Bank Negara Malaysia is most honored to host this year’s summit, which is held in conjunction with the 10th anniversary of the Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB). It was here in Kuala Lumpur 10 years ago that we witnessed the momentous occasion of the IFSB inauguration, that was the culmination of international collaboration among the founding member countries with the support of several key international and multilateral institutions. Its landmark establishment in 2002 as the international prudential standard setting body for the Islamic finance marked a major milestone in the effort to strengthen the international infrastructure for the Islamic financial system, steering the path for its successful integration as a viable component of the global financial system. A decade on, the work of the IFSB in ensuring a cohesive cross-border regulatory framework and the international best practices that are attuned to the intrinsic characteristics and peculiarities of Islamic financial intermediation, have served to underpin the development of a sound and stable Islamic financial system, ushering in a phase of rapid growth and greater internationalization of the industry.
Indeed, 10 years since the founding of the IFSB have been a period of significance, during which the Islamic financial services industry has grown impressively with its landscape dramatically evolved. This growth acceleration has been accompanied by the widening of its geographical reach transcending its traditional borders in Muslim majority countries to the more established financial centres. In addition, Islamic finance has evolved as a comprehensive system of intermediation servicing all segments of society, including governments, businesses and households regardless of scale of businesses and income levels. In this decade, Islamic finance has also evolved from being domestic-centric to become increasingly internationalized, intermediating funds across borders and becoming a new vehicle that bridges economies and fostering closer financial linkages, particularly among emerging and developing markets.
As a form of financial intermediation that is well anchored to serve the real economy, Islamic finance offers distinct potential to achieve the goals of inclusive growth and financial stability. Its foundations have been strengthened with the setting up of the IFSB and before that, the Accounting and Auditing Organisation for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI), have taken the lead in setting the prudential and accounting standards for the industry. Combined with continuous capacity building initiatives and institutional development, it has resulted in the opportunity to achieve scale and has allowed the Islamic financial services industry to transition into a dynamic, fast growing and competitive form of financial intermediation for the global community.
The IFSB today is celebrating its tenth anniversary in a world which is changing profoundly. A new growth and development agenda is unfolding before us. Given the severe damage and devastation caused by the global financial crisis and the ensuing economic downturns, the road to an enduring recovery and lasting prosperity demands a global policy response that brings about a new economic trajectory built on a strong, more inclusive and more sustainable growth path. Common challenges that have also come to the forefront, such as poverty, increasing inequality and the imperative for greater social cohesion, have also called for the construction of policy objectives and strategies that can enhance stability, social well-being and environmental sustainability. In the wake of the global financial crisis, there is consensus on the need for a return to financial systems that serve the real economy, and the demands for more responsible financial practices from the financial sector, that also includes the commitment to achieve socio-economic goals.
In response, the international community is prioritizing financial stability by strengthening financial regulation. This includes financial reforms aimed at protecting depositors from excessive risk-taking, over-leveraging and unfettered innovation. The reform initiatives have also focused on enhancing capital and liquidity standards, reinforced by moves to strengthen the macro-prudential orientation of regulation to complement micro-prudential supervision to manage the risks arising from the interdependencies within the financial system. Whilst the breadth of regulatory changes being considered collectively endeavor to strengthen financial system resilience, the key challenge for policymakers and regulators going forward is also to achieve
inclusive
and more sustainable
growth,
whilst ensuring
financial stability.
Whilst Islamic finance has benefited from a well developed, more competitive and well regulated eco-system, it needs to build on and reinforce the solid foundations that has been achieved in this decade. As the industry transitions into a new era of growth and development in this post-crisis world, the competitive financial landscape is being redrawn by the evolving international regulatory reforms, changing operating models, rising consumer expectations and increased competition. In this more challenging environment, the success of sustaining the momentum of Islamic finance as a transformative agent for the economy, will hinge on the ability to
keep raising the bar in the pursuit of an effective functioning and sound Islamic financial system
.
Post-crisis, the increased emphasis for inclusive and sustainable products as well as responsible corporate behavior provides clear potential for Islamic financial players to demonstrate leadership by capitalizing on core value propositions of Islamic financial intermediation. There is also scope for greater leverage on the advances of technology and new institutional arrangements that can enhance operational excellence, particularly distribution channels for extending outreach to the range of users from households to microenterprises and small and medium scale enterprises.
In addition, innovations in Islamic financial solutions will need to take into account the higher regulatory expectations for more transparency, and the need for the effective management of risks and capital. This involves strengthening the resilience of the Islamic financial system in alignment with the evolving international regulatory developments thus raising the bar of industry performance. The IFSB has made significant advancements in leading the efforts to review specific measures put forward by the Basel Committee for possible adoption in Islamic finance. Further to this is the imperative to cultivate a strong risk culture within institutions. Reinforced by a robust shariah governance framework, it will ensure that innovation for furthering the development of Islamic finance is harnessed within the boundaries of the Shariah, which would avert overzealous innovative activities that could undermine financial stability.
Let me conclude my remarks. Much has been achieved, both in terms of the role and contribution of the IFSB, and the advancement made by Islamic finance in this recent decade. This has been an outcome of cumulative efforts to strengthen the foundations of the Islamic financial system. As the industry gears itself for the next phase of growth in the more challenging environment, our commitment and strategies to keep raising the bar to bring Islamic finance to a new level will enhance its prospect to contribute to achieving our shared vision of inclusive growth in an environment of financial stability.
title: Governor’s Welcoming Address at the 10th IFSB Summit 2013 - The Future of the Islamic Financial Services Industry: Resilience, Stability and Inclusive Growth

Speech by Assistant Governor at the Launch of e-Banking Fraud Awareness Campaign
Speaker
: Encik Abu Hassan Alshari Yahaya
Venue
: Sasana Kijang, Kuala Lumpur
Delivery Date
:
15 Jan. 2013
It is my pleasure and honour to be invited to launch this joint e-Banking fraud awareness campaign. I would like to thank the Association of Banks in Malaysia for this invitation and the coordinated efforts in undertaking this important awareness campaign.
A significant initiative
This campaign is indeed a very important initiative for the banking industry in Malaysia. This is the first time that all banks have come together in a concerted effort to help create greater awareness of online fraud with the cooperation of CyberSecurity and the Police Force. This is to be lauded as all stakeholders have a role to play in preserving the safety and security of the banking system.
Maintaining confidence in online banking services
Online transactions have been growing at a rapid pace over the years. Over the last decade, the use of electronic payments has increased at an average annual growth of 23.4%. In 2012, Malaysian households and businesses performed more than 300 million financial transactions with a value close to RM15 trillion via electronic channels comprising mainly funds transfers, bill payments, top-up for prepaid cards, purchases of phone cards and payments for investments in the capital market. Among the electronic channels, internet banking is the most popular.
Fundamental to the growth of internet banking over the years is the confidence which the public has in its convenience and security. This is something that we cannot take for granted and must be continuously preserved. Advancement in technology and innovation has resulted in greater consumer convenience and enhanced efficiency. However, the same technology and innovation have also created new methods of perpetrating fraud that could be executed faster and with greater reach. Cyber criminals have been active ever since the advent of the internet, and are constantly finding new ways to defraud innocent victims.
Safety and security of transactions in the banking system is fundamental in ensuring consumer confidence. Hence, an important function and responsibility of the Central Bank is to ensure online transactions can be made in a safe and efficient manner in the economy, in the pursuit of monetary and financial stability objectives.
The need for constant vigilance & cooperation
This fight that the banks are launching today is something that requires the support of all parties. We are aware of the creative ways in which criminals have attempted to deceive customers over the years and measures were required to be taken by the banks to protect the customers. While it is good to know that banks have played their roles in investing in robust security systems, they must also ensure that customers play their part in protecting their own assets and savings.
The reminder and greater awareness from the Banks through this campaign is timely. It will not only reinforce the need for constant vigilance from all parties, but also help create an environment where everyone is risk conscious and responsible in protecting the interests of each other. These initiatives would not achieve the desired outcomes without effective communication, and the media has a critical role to play in conveying the message from the banks. We have always acknowledged the importance of the media and I would like to record Bank Negara Malaysia’s appreciation for the assistance rendered by the media in creating awareness of this issue in the past. We hope that with the support of the media on this occasion too, this campaign will be a success, and the public will have heightened levels of understanding and vigilance over this issue.
On behalf of Bank Negara Malaysia, I would like to thank all the banks for taking this initiative to undertake this joint e-banking awareness campaign. Our thanks also to Cyber Security and the Police Force for your ongoing efforts to collaborate with the banking industry. I wish all of you the best and assure you that Bank Negara Malaysia will continuously support you in this noble effort.
title: Speech by Assistant Governor at the Launch of e-Banking Fraud Awareness Campaign
